reports.label: CPO / Threat Defense: Reimagining Operations Through Preemptive Cybersecurity (v3 — 86-Vendor Updated)
reports.title: Market Insight: Reimagining Threat Defense Operations and Engineering Through Preemptive Cybersecurity
reports.summary: An expanded 86-vendor assessment of the preemptive cybersecurity market, analyzed through the dual lens of the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK, reveals a market in the early stages of a structural transition—but with critical capability gaps that most vendors have not yet closed. Four defensive pillars map directly to adversary lifecycle phases: Exposure Management (kill chain Phase 1, ATT&CK Reconnaissance), Adversary Management (Phases 1–2, Resource Development and Defense Evasion), Posture and Policy Management (Phases 2–3, Initial Access), and Adversary Disruption (Phases 4–7, Execution through Impact). Services and Capability Maturity operates as the cross-cutting enablement layer determining how effectively each pillar is operationalized. Across 86 vendors, Adversary Management remains the critical bottleneck: only 16% of vendors score above the competency threshold on this pillar, and no vendor in the cohort achieves a score of 2.5 or above—meaning the market’s earliest-phase preemptive capability is both broadly absent and uniformly shallow. Fewer than 6% of vendors achieve meaningful coverage across all four defensive pillars. Services maturity scores have expanded across vendor types but remain uneven, with 41% of vendors meeting the services competency threshold and only 16% demonstrating platform-level services depth. For CPOs, the window to differentiate on genuine shift-left positioning remains open but is narrowing as the vendor universe expands and buyer frameworks mature.
reports.spa: By 2028, 40% of enterprise preemptive cybersecurity evaluations will use adversary lifecycle phase coverage—mapped to kill chain phases or MITRE ATT&CK tactics—as a primary vendor selection criterion, up from less than 10% today. The Adversary Management gap will define competitive separation: no vendor in the current 86-vendor cohort has achieved the 2.5 threshold on this pillar, creating a clear first-mover advantage for any product organization that prioritizes polymorphic defense, moving target defense, and credential rotation investment. Services maturity will increasingly function as the delivery multiplier that separates technology capability from operational defensive value, particularly as the cohort expands to include SaaS-only, managed services, and consulting-led vendors whose technology strength varies widely.

findings.header: Adversary Management is the critical bottleneck across all 86 vendors—only 16% clear the competency threshold, and the 2.5 ceiling remains unclaimed.
findings.body: In the expanded 86-vendor cohort, Adversary Management records the lowest penetration among all five pillars and the only pillar where no vendor achieves a score of 2.5 or above. Only 13 of 81 scored vendors (16%) meet the 2.0 competency threshold, compared to 49% for Exposure Management, 41% for Services maturity, 37% for Posture and Policy Management, and 33% for Adversary Disruption. In kill chain terms, this means Phases 1 and 2—Reconnaissance and Weaponization—are the least defended stages across the entire market. In ATT&CK terms, Resource Development (TA0042), Defense Evasion (TA0005), and Credential Access (TA0006) receive the weakest defensive attention of any tactic category. The competitive implication is stark: the first vendor cohort to push Adversary Management scores above 2.5 will occupy defensive territory that no current competitor holds. The capabilities required—polymorphic defense, moving target infrastructure, runtime application protection, and automated credential rotation—are technically demanding but not inaccessible. They represent the highest-leverage investment in the preemptive cybersecurity stack for any CPO seeking differentiated positioning.

findings.header: Full-spectrum coverage has declined sharply as the vendor universe expanded: fewer than 6% of vendors achieve meaningful coverage across all four defensive pillars.
findings.body: In earlier assessments of 51 core vendors, approximately 27% achieved full-spectrum coverage across the four defensive pillars (Exposure Management, Adversary Management, Posture and Policy Management, and Adversary Disruption each scoring 2.0 or above). Expanding the cohort to 86 vendors—adding SaaS platforms, managed service providers, consulting-led vendors, and specialized point-solution providers—reveals that full-spectrum coverage is far less common across the broader market: only 5 of 86 vendors (5.8%) clear the threshold on all four pillars. This is not a regression in quality among the original cohort but a reflection of the structural diversity of the expanded market, where many vendors deliver strong performance on one or two pillars while leaving the others unaddressed. An additional 9 vendors achieve full-spectrum coverage on three of four pillars, with Adversary Management as the exclusive gap. Together, these 14 vendors (16.3%) represent the highest tier of the market—those that have made real progress toward full-lifecycle defense but are held back by the single most critical bottleneck in the preemptive stack.

findings.header: The four defensive pillars map consistently to both kill chain phases and ATT&CK tactics, validating the dual-framework lens across the expanded cohort.
findings.body: Mapping the five-pillar preemptive cybersecurity taxonomy to both the Lockheed Martin Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK confirms the structural logic of both frameworks across 86 vendors. Exposure Management addresses kill chain Phase 1 and ATT&CK Reconnaissance (TA0043) and Discovery (TA0007)—the phase with the broadest vendor coverage (49.4% at 2.0 or above). Adversary Management spans Phases 1 and 2 and ATT&CK Resource Development (TA0042), Defense Evasion (TA0005), and Credential Access (TA0006)—the phase with the narrowest coverage (16.0%). Posture and Policy Management validates defenses at Phases 2 and 3, mapping to Initial Access (TA0001) and Privilege Escalation (TA0004)—36.6% of vendors at threshold. Adversary Disruption covers Phases 4 through 7, mapping to Execution (TA0002), Persistence (TA0003), Lateral Movement (TA0008), Command and Control (TA0011), Collection (TA0009), Exfiltration (TA0010), and Impact (TA0040)—32.9% of vendors at threshold. Services and Capability Maturity operates as a cross-cutting enablement layer across all phases, with 41.2% of vendors at threshold. The pattern holds regardless of which framework is applied: the preemptive zone (Phases 1–2 / Reconnaissance through Resource Development) is the weakest-defended region of the adversary lifecycle across the full cohort.

findings.header: Services maturity is the cross-cutting differentiator, but the expanded cohort reveals its uneven distribution across vendor types.
findings.body: Services and Capability Maturity does not map to specific adversary lifecycle phases—it is the enablement layer that determines whether any pillar’s capability is actually operationalized. Across 86 vendors, 41.2% score at or above the 2.0 competency threshold on Services maturity, with 16.2% reaching the 2.5 platform-services level. The 41% figure is higher than any individual defensive pillar except Exposure Management, confirming that services delivery is a relative strength for vendors who prioritize it. However, the expanded cohort introduces significant variability: SaaS-only platforms, point-solution providers, and early-stage vendors that were not in the original 51 frequently show strong technology scores paired with low services maturity, producing the classic gap between capability and operational effectiveness. For enterprise buyers, this reinforces the principle that technology capability and service delivery must be evaluated together. A vendor scoring 2.5 on Exposure Management but 1.0 on Services maturity will produce far less defensive value in practice than one scoring 2.0 on both dimensions.

findings.header: The expanded cohort reveals three distinct vendor archetypes that determine adversary lifecycle phase coverage patterns.
findings.body: The 86-vendor cohort encompasses three primary vendor archetypes that produce different adversary lifecycle coverage profiles. Technology-led platform vendors (typically SaaS or on-premises platforms) show the strongest Exposure Management and Posture and Policy Management scores but consistently fall below competency thresholds on Adversary Management and Services maturity. Their kill chain coverage concentrates in Phases 1 and 2–3 on the technology side, with Phases 5–7 largely unaddressed. Service-and-consulting-led vendors (managed services, systems integrators, advisory firms) tend to show the strongest Services maturity and Adversary Disruption scores, reflecting their operational depth and incident response heritage, while Exposure Management and Adversary Management are often secondary priorities. Integrated platform-plus-service vendors—those combining technology depth with managed operations—produce the most balanced coverage across all phases, but represent a minority of the cohort. The presence of all three archetypes in a single 86-vendor assessment underscores why delivery model classification matters as much as pillar scores when evaluating vendor kill chain coverage: the same numerical score can represent fundamentally different operational realities depending on how a vendor delivers its capability.

findings.header: MITRE ATT&CK tactic coverage mirrors the kill chain gap pattern, with Resource Development and Defense Evasion the most underserved adversary objectives.
findings.body: MITRE ATT&CK’s tactic-level granularity confirms what kill chain phase analysis reveals at the phase level. Reconnaissance (TA0043) is the best-covered ATT&CK tactic, with Exposure Management providing broad attack surface visibility. Initial Access (TA0001) benefits from the convergence of Exposure Management, Posture and Policy Management, and early Adversary Disruption capabilities. But Resource Development (TA0042)—where adversaries build infrastructure, develop exploits, and obtain tooling—and Defense Evasion (TA0005)—where adversaries neutralize defensive controls—remain the weakest-covered tactics in the cohort, with Adversary Management as the only pillar that addresses them. Credential Access (TA0006), dependent on identity and credential rotation within Adversary Management, is also poorly covered. The late-phase tactics—Lateral Movement (TA0008), Collection (TA0009), Exfiltration (TA0010), and Command and Control (TA0011)—benefit from Adversary Disruption coverage but effectiveness varies directly with Services maturity: vendors with strong managed operations deliver measurably faster detection and containment, while platform-only vendors with weak services leave customers to independently operate complex detection tools.

recommendations.header: Map your current portfolio against kill chain phases and ATT&CK tactics using the five-pillar framework to expose structural coverage gaps.
recommendations.body: CPOs should conduct a dual-framework mapping exercise against both the seven-phase kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK’s 14 enterprise tactics, using the five-pillar taxonomy as the mapping bridge. For each phase and tactic, identify which product capabilities provide measurable defense and score them honestly against the 2.0 competency threshold. Any kill chain phase or ATT&CK tactic where coverage falls below threshold represents a structural gap that limits competitive positioning. This exercise should be conducted with delivery model specificity: the same technology capability produces different adversary lifecycle coverage depending on whether it is delivered as a SaaS platform, a managed service, or an integrated advisory-plus-technology offering. Document the results as a coverage heat map that can be used in product investment cases, competitive positioning, and customer-facing value demonstrations.

recommendations.header: Treat Adversary Management as the single highest-leverage investment for shift-left differentiation—no vendor in the market has claimed the 2.5 threshold.
recommendations.body: The data presents an unambiguous opportunity: no vendor across 86 assessed organizations has achieved a score of 2.5 or above on Adversary Management. The specific capabilities required—polymorphic and morphing defense that changes the attack surface dynamically, runtime application self-protection that blocks exploitation without signature dependence, dynamic network and infrastructure defense that invalidates adversary reconnaissance, and identity and credential rotation that renders stolen access worthless within hours—map directly to ATT&CK Resource Development (TA0042), Defense Evasion (TA0005), and Credential Access (TA0006). These are the tactics where the market is least prepared and where enterprise buyers are most exposed. A CPO who drives Adversary Management scores above 2.5 differentiates in a category no competitor currently occupies. That differentiation is durable because these capabilities require deep systems engineering expertise—runtime instrumentation, network-level manipulation, and cryptographic automation—that cannot be acquired quickly.

recommendations.header: Reframe product positioning around adversary lifecycle phase coverage rather than feature catalogs.
recommendations.body: Enterprise security leaders increasingly evaluate vendors through adversary framework lenses—MITRE ATT&CK, kill chain phase mapping, NIST CSF functions. Yet most preemptive cybersecurity vendors still market as feature catalogs that buyers must map to their own frameworks. CPOs should restructure product marketing and sales engineering to explicitly show which kill chain phases and ATT&CK tactics each product addresses, what percentage of adversary techniques are disrupted at each phase, and the measurable outcome difference between preemptive intervention at Phases 1–3 versus reactive response at Phases 5–7. This reframing converts a technical procurement conversation into a strategic risk conversation. Vendors who adopt adversary lifecycle messaging first establish the evaluation framework that competitors must then compete within. Given that no vendor currently dominates the Adversary Management narrative, the first to claim it credibly will own the most valuable messaging position in the market.

recommendations.header: Invest in Services maturity as the cross-cutting amplifier across all four defensive pillars—not as a standalone service line.
recommendations.body: Services and Capability Maturity is not about adding a managed service offering on the right side of the kill chain. It is the operational layer that determines whether every defensive pillar—from Exposure Management at Phase 1 through Adversary Disruption at Phase 7—is delivered with enough operational depth to produce defensive results. CPOs should invest across all four services maturity dimensions: implementation and onboarding that ensures comprehensive, rapid deployment; consultative and advisory services that translate capability findings into customer action; managed operations and continuous delivery that run the technology with expert oversight around the clock; and autonomous service delivery that scales operational expertise through AI-driven automation. The 86-vendor data shows that services maturity scores are meaningfully correlated with full-spectrum coverage—vendors that invest in operational depth are disproportionately represented among the 14 vendors that approach or achieve coverage across all phases. Neglecting services maturity in favor of technology depth alone produces a widening gap between what a product can theoretically do and what it delivers in the field.

recommendations.header: Use delivery model classification as a first-order vendor differentiation criterion in competitive analysis and customer positioning.
recommendations.body: The 86-vendor cohort encompasses a wider range of delivery models than any prior assessment—SaaS platforms, managed service providers, consulting-led firms, systems integrators, and integrated platform-plus-service vendors. Each delivery model produces a structurally different kill chain coverage profile. Technology-platform vendors concentrate coverage in Phases 1–3 but leave Phases 5–7 dependent on customer operations capacity. Service-and-consulting vendors provide strong Phase 5–7 coverage but may under-invest in Phase 1–2 technology depth. Integrated vendors achieve the most complete coverage but are rarest. CPOs should classify both their own organization and key competitors by delivery model before conducting phase-coverage comparisons—a direct comparison of scores between a pure SaaS platform and a managed services firm is analytically misleading if delivery model differences are not controlled for. Competitive positioning should lead with delivery model: customers evaluating across archetypes need help understanding why their coverage profile will differ depending not just on which vendor they choose, but on what kind of vendor.

analysis_sections.title: The Dual Framework Lens: Kill Chain and ATT&CK Across 86 Vendors
analysis_sections.body:
The Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain describes seven sequential phases that adversaries must complete to achieve their objective: Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, and Actions on Objectives. MITRE ATT&CK complements this linear model with 14 enterprise tactics—Reconnaissance, Resource Development, Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defense Evasion, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Collection, Exfiltration, Command and Control, and Impact—each described through hundreds of specific techniques observed in real-world adversary campaigns.

Together, these frameworks provide a multi-resolution lens for defensive coverage analysis: kill chain at the phase level, ATT&CK at the tactic and technique level. The preemptive cybersecurity taxonomy maps cleanly to both. Exposure Management addresses kill chain Phase 1 and ATT&CK Reconnaissance (TA0043) and Discovery (TA0007). Adversary Management spans Phases 1 and 2 and ATT&CK Resource Development (TA0042), Defense Evasion (TA0005), and Credential Access (TA0006). Posture and Policy Management covers Phases 2 and 3 and ATT&CK Initial Access (TA0001) and Privilege Escalation (TA0004). Adversary Disruption covers Phases 4 through 7 and the post-exploitation ATT&CK tactics from Execution (TA0002) through Impact (TA0040). Services and Capability Maturity does not map to any specific phase or tactic—it is the cross-cutting operational layer that determines whether the technology capability registered in each pillar translates into actual defensive coverage at every phase.

Applying this mapping to 86 vendors produces a comprehensive view of market coverage across the full adversary lifecycle. The findings are consistent with prior assessments of 51 vendors but more revealing at the extremes: expanding the cohort to include SaaS platforms, managed service providers, consulting firms, and specialized point-solution vendors confirms and amplifies the core structural gap identified previously—the preemptive zone is systematically underserved, and Adversary Management remains the single most critical unclaimed capability in the market.

analysis_sections.title: Adversary Lifecycle Coverage: The 86-Vendor Coverage Map
analysis_sections.body:
Mapping 86 vendor pillar scores to kill chain phases and ATT&CK tactics reveals a coverage gradient that declines sharply in the earliest adversary phases.

Exposure Management—covering kill chain Phase 1 and ATT&CK Reconnaissance—achieves the highest market penetration among the four defensive pillars, with 41 of 83 scored vendors (49.4%) meeting the 2.0 competency threshold and a market mean of 1.84. This reflects broad investment in attack surface management, vulnerability prioritization, and third-party risk visibility across the cohort, including both established platform vendors and newer SaaS-native offerings.

Adversary Management—covering kill chain Phases 1 and 2 and ATT&CK Resource Development, Defense Evasion, and Credential Access—records the lowest penetration of the four defensive pillars. Only 13 of 81 scored vendors (16.0%) reach the 2.0 threshold, the market mean is 1.13, and no vendor in the cohort reaches 2.5. This is the market’s most critical defensive gap: the adversary lifecycle phases where preemptive investment would have the highest incident-prevention return are the phases where market supply is thinnest.

Posture and Policy Management—covering kill chain Phases 2 and 3 and ATT&CK Initial Access and Privilege Escalation—reaches 30 of 82 vendors (36.6%) at threshold, with a market mean of 1.67. Breach and attack simulation, control validation, and cloud security posture management are present in meaningful percentages of the cohort but have not yet achieved broad penetration.

Adversary Disruption—covering kill chain Phases 4 through 7 and ATT&CK Execution through Impact—reaches 27 of 82 vendors (32.9%) at threshold, with a market mean of 1.47. Deception, threat hunting, counter-adversary operations, and managed incident response capabilities are present but variable in depth across the cohort.

Services and Capability Maturity—the cross-cutting enablement layer—reaches 33 of 80 vendors (41.2%) at the 2.0 threshold and 13 of 80 (16.2%) at the 2.5 platform-services level, with a market mean of 1.80. The 41% services penetration rate, higher than Adversary Management, Adversary Disruption, and Posture Management, suggests that operational delivery capability is available in the market but not uniformly matched to technology strength.

Full-spectrum vendors—those meeting the 2.0 threshold across all four defensive pillars—number 5 of 86 (5.8%). An additional 9 vendors are near-full-spectrum with Adversary Management as the only pillar below threshold. These 14 vendors (16.3% of the cohort) represent the leading edge of the preemptive cybersecurity market.

analysis_sections.title: The Adversary Management Bottleneck: Anatomy of an Unclaimed Market Position
analysis_sections.body:
Adversary Management is the preemptive cybersecurity pillar most directly responsible for shift-left defense—disrupting adversaries before they can deliver a weapon. Its four core sub-capabilities each address specific adversary preparation mechanisms across both frameworks.

Polymorphic and morphing defense dynamically changes the appearance and structure of the defended environment, invalidating adversary reconnaissance data. In kill chain terms this disrupts Phase 1 (Reconnaissance). In ATT&CK terms it counters Active Scanning (T1595) and Gather Victim Network Information (T1590) within the Reconnaissance tactic (TA0043).

Runtime application self-protection blocks exploitation attempts at the application layer without signature dependence, operating at Phase 2 (Weaponization) and Phase 4 (Exploitation) in kill chain terms and countering Defense Evasion (TA0005) techniques including Process Injection (T1055) and Obfuscated Files (T1027).

Dynamic network and infrastructure defense uses moving target principles to continuously alter network topology, addresses, and service configurations, frustrating adversary delivery and Command and Control establishment. This spans kill chain Phases 1, 3, and 6, and ATT&CK Command and Control (TA0011) and Delivery-phase Initial Access techniques.

Identity and credential rotation automates the rotation of credentials, API tokens, and session identifiers, rendering stolen access worthless within hours of theft. This disrupts kill chain Phases 2, 4, and 6 and counters ATT&CK Credential Access (TA0006) techniques including Brute Force (T1110) and OS Credential Dumping (T1003).

The 86-vendor data confirms that these capabilities represent the hardest and most sparsely deployed in the preemptive stack. No vendor achieves a 2.5 score on Adversary Management—the threshold that signals meaningful operational deployment of two or more of these capabilities at enterprise scale. This is the clearest product-market gap identified in the full-cohort assessment, and it maps directly to the adversary lifecycle phases (Phases 1 and 2, ATT&CK Resource Development and Weaponization) where intervention yields the highest prevention return. For CPOs, this represents an unambiguous and currently unoccupied competitive position.

analysis_sections.title: Services Maturity as the Operational Multiplier Across All Adversary Phases
analysis_sections.body:
The most consequential finding from the 86-vendor assessment is not which adversary phases are best or worst covered—it is the degree to which Services and Capability Maturity determines whether technology coverage is operationally real or theoretically registered.

Services maturity encompasses four dimensions. Implementation and onboarding determines how quickly and completely a vendor’s technology capability is deployed to achieve first defensive value. Consultative and advisory services determine whether findings and detections are translated into actionable customer decisions. Managed operations and continuous delivery determine whether defensive tools run with expert oversight or depend on the customer’s own operational capacity. Autonomous service delivery determines how effectively AI-driven automation scales expert-level operations to match adversary tempo.

Vendors with mature service delivery achieve a compounding advantage across the adversary lifecycle. Their Exposure Management findings become remediation programs rather than reports. Their Adversary Disruption detections trigger managed response rather than alert queues. Their Posture and Policy Management simulations generate validated control configurations rather than gap documentation. Services maturity does not change what a vendor can do—it changes what a vendor actually delivers.

The 86-vendor cohort exhibits a wider services maturity distribution than earlier assessments of the core 51 vendors, reflecting the expanded inclusion of SaaS-only platforms (typically lower services maturity) and managed service providers and consulting firms (typically higher). At 41.2% penetration at the 2.0 threshold and 16.2% at 2.5, services maturity is better distributed than most defensive pillars, but the gap between technology scores and services scores on individual vendors is often large. The strategic implication: CPOs at platform-oriented vendors must either invest in services maturity as a product capability or accept that their technology capability scores will consistently outperform their delivered defensive value—a gap that sophisticated buyers increasingly detect and discount in evaluations.

analysis_sections.title: Delivery Model Archetypes and Their Kill Chain Profiles
analysis_sections.body:
The 86-vendor cohort encompasses a wider range of delivery models than any prior assessment, including models that did not appear in earlier evaluations of the core 51 vendors. Three classic delivery model archetypes—Platform-Only, Direct Service, and Platform-Plus-Partner—account for approximately 60% of the cohort. The remaining 40% includes SaaS platforms, managed service providers, systems integrators, consulting and advisory firms, and hybrid models that do not fit cleanly into the three classic categories.

Platform-Only vendors (25 in the cohort) show the highest Posture and Policy Management means (1.90) and moderate Exposure Management (1.86), consistent with their investment in technology-led control validation and attack surface visibility. Adversary Management (1.15) and Services maturity (1.42) are both below threshold, confirming the structural limitation of platform-only delivery: strong Phases 1 and 3 coverage, weak Phase 2 and Phases 5–7 capability. Only 3 of 25 platform-only vendors meet the Adversary Management threshold.

Direct Service vendors (11 in the cohort) show the strongest Adversary Disruption scores (1.91) and Services maturity (1.82) among the three archetypes, reflecting their analyst-intensive service delivery heritage. Exposure Management (1.74) and Posture and Policy Management (1.72) are lower, suggesting that while these vendors defend well in the reactive zone (Phases 4–7), they underinvest in early-phase preemptive capabilities. Adversary Management (1.17) remains below threshold even for direct service providers.

Platform-Plus-Partner vendors (15 in the cohort) show strong Services maturity (1.90) and Exposure Management (1.89), with lower Posture and Policy Management (1.37) and Adversary Disruption (1.47). Their model—combining platform technology with MSSP partner delivery—produces competitive early-phase coverage but inconsistent reactive-phase performance depending on partner quality and integration depth.

The additional 35 vendors in newer delivery model categories exhibit the full range of pillar profiles: some SaaS platforms show strong single-pillar scores with weak coverage elsewhere, while managed service and consulting-led vendors often show the reverse pattern. This heterogeneity reinforces the need for delivery-model-aware evaluation rather than aggregate score comparisons.

analysis_sections.title: Strategic Roadmap: Building Full Adversary Lifecycle Coverage in a 86-Vendor Market
analysis_sections.body:
The expansion from 51 to 86 assessed vendors changes the competitive context for CPOs without changing the underlying strategic priorities. The adversary lifecycle gaps identified in earlier assessments are confirmed and amplified by the larger cohort, and the first-mover advantages available to CPOs who close those gaps remain unclaimed.

Phase 1 (2026), Portfolio Mapping and Gap Quantification: Conduct a dual-framework mapping exercise to score your current portfolio against kill chain phases and ATT&CK tactics. Separately assess services maturity across all four dimensions. Identify all phases and tactics below the 2.0 threshold. Benchmark against the 86-vendor cohort means: EXM 1.84, AMT 1.13, ADR 1.47, PPM 1.67, SVC 1.80. Any pillar above these means represents relative strength; any below represents a structural drag on competitive positioning.

Phase 2 (2026 to 2027), Adversary Management Investment: Prioritize investment in the four Adversary Management sub-capabilities. Target at least 2.0 threshold performance to join the 16% of vendors who have cleared that bar, and set a 2.5 target to achieve a position no competitor currently holds. Simultaneously invest in services maturity to ensure new Adversary Management capabilities are operationally delivered—technology capability without operational depth produces scores but not results.

Phase 3 (2027 to 2028), Adversary Lifecycle Positioning: Develop go-to-market messaging around kill chain phase coverage and ATT&CK tactic addressing. Build customer-facing metrics (Shift-Left Readiness Index, ATT&CK Coverage Score) that translate internal capability investments into buyer-visible outcomes. Position full adversary lifecycle coverage as the competitive standard.

Success Metrics by 2028: Adversary Management score above 2.5 (currently unoccupied). Services maturity score above 2.5 (achieved by 16% of the cohort). Full-spectrum coverage (all four defensive pillars at 2.0 or above)—currently 5.8% of the market. Customer-facing adversary lifecycle phase coverage metrics deployed across sales, marketing, and renewal conversations.

reports.background:
The Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain provides a seven-phase model of adversary behavior widely adopted by security operations teams, threat intelligence analysts, and enterprise security architects. Originally developed to analyze advanced persistent threats, the kill chain framework has become the common language for describing how attacks progress from initial reconnaissance through mission completion. The MITRE ATT&CK framework complements the kill chain with a globally accessible knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations. Its 14 enterprise tactics, mapped to hundreds of specific techniques, provide the granular detail needed to evaluate defensive coverage at the technique level.

The preemptive cybersecurity market has emerged as a category distinct from traditional detection-and-response solutions. Defined by four defensive pillars (Exposure Management, Adversary Management and Threat Intelligence, Posture and Policy Management, and Adversary Disruption) and a cross-cutting enablement layer (Services and Capability Maturity), preemptive cybersecurity aims to neutralize threats before they cause damage rather than detecting and remediating after the fact.

This version of the market insight updates the analysis from an earlier 51-vendor assessment to reflect an expanded 86-vendor cohort that includes the original evaluated vendors plus a broader range of vendor types: SaaS-native platforms, managed service providers, systems integrators, consulting and advisory firms, and specialized point-solution providers. The expanded cohort provides a more complete picture of the commercial market and surfaces structural dynamics that the smaller, more curated original cohort did not fully expose.
reports.impact:
For Chief Product Officers and Product Strategy Leaders:

The 86-vendor assessment confirms and sharpens the strategic imperatives identified in earlier assessments. CPOs face three immediate implications:

1. Portfolio Reassessment at Scale: The benchmark for competitive adequacy has shifted. In a 51-vendor cohort where 27% of vendors achieved full-spectrum coverage, the threshold felt achievable. In an 86-vendor cohort where only 5.8% achieve full-spectrum coverage, the bar is clearly higher and the challenge is structural. CPOs must evaluate their pillar scores not against an idealized threshold but against the actual distribution of the expanded market—where EXM 1.84 is the mean, AMT 1.13 is the mean, and no vendor has claimed a 2.5 on Adversary Management.

2. Adversary Management as Primary Investment Priority: With 0 of 86 vendors above 2.5 on Adversary Management, this is the clearest unoccupied competitive position in the market. The investment case is straightforward: the capabilities required are technically defined, the competitive position is unclaimed, and buyer demand for earliest-phase preemptive defense is increasing as MITRE ATT&CK evaluations mature.

3. Services Maturity as a Mandatory Investment: The expanded cohort includes many vendors with strong technology scores and weak operational delivery. In a buyer market that increasingly evaluates vendors on outcome delivery rather than feature capability, services maturity investment is no longer optional. CPOs who deprioritize services maturity in favor of technology feature velocity will find their measured capability scores increasingly disconnected from buyer-perceived value.

For Technology and Engineering Leaders:

Engineering roadmaps should prioritize the four Adversary Management sub-capabilities (polymorphic defense, runtime application protection, dynamic infrastructure defense, credential rotation) as technically demanding but strategically critical investments. These capabilities require systems-level expertise in runtime instrumentation, network manipulation, and cryptographic automation—skills that cannot be acquired through product management decisions alone and represent durable competitive moats.

For Corporate Development and Strategy Leaders:

Acquisition strategy should target the Adversary Management gap as the primary value-creation thesis. Any acquisition that delivers credible capability above the 2.0 threshold on Adversary Management creates cross-pillar value by enabling full-spectrum positioning. Secondary acquisition value lies in services maturity—acquisitions that add managed operations depth amplify the delivered value of every existing technology pillar simultaneously.
reports.conclusion:
Expanding the preemptive cybersecurity assessment to 86 vendors confirms the structural thesis while sharpening its edge. The kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK dual-framework analysis reveals a market that is growing in scale and vendor diversity but not yet in the depth of capability that defines genuine shift-left defense. Exposure Management has achieved meaningful market penetration. Services maturity is present in over 40% of the cohort. But Adversary Management—the pillar that addresses the earliest and most prevention-valuable adversary lifecycle phases—remains at 16% penetration with no vendor at the 2.5 threshold.

For CPOs, the strategic imperative is unchanged from prior assessments but more urgent: the window for first-mover advantage on Adversary Management is open, the competitive space is unoccupied, and the buyer demand for genuine preemptive—not just pre-detection—capability is accelerating. Services maturity investment remains the force multiplier that converts technology capability into defensible market positioning.

The vendors who will define the next generation of preemptive cybersecurity are not those with the broadest feature catalogs or the largest vendor cohort coverage scores. They are those that combine genuine Adversary Management capability—disrupting adversaries at Phases 1 and 2, countering Resource Development and Defense Evasion—with the operational services depth to deliver those capabilities reliably at enterprise scale. In an 86-vendor market where full-spectrum coverage remains below 6%, the competitive ceiling is still unclaimed.

Adversary Management spans Phases 1 and 2 and ATT&CK Resource Development (TA0042), Defense Evasion (TA0005), and Credential Access (TA0006). Posture and Policy Management covers Phases 2 and 3 and ATT&CK Initial Access (TA0001) and Privilege Escalation (TA0004). Adversary Disruption covers Phases 4 through 7 and the post-exploitation ATT&CK tactics from Execution (TA0002) through Impact (TA0040). Services and Capability Maturity does not map to any specific phase or tactic—it is the cross-cutting operational layer that determines whether the technology capability registered in each pillar translates into actual defensive coverage at every phase.

Applying this mapping to 86 vendors produces a comprehensive view of market coverage across the full adversary lifecycle. The findings are consistent with prior assessments of 51 vendors but more revealing at the extremes: expanding the cohort to include SaaS platforms, managed service providers, consulting firms, and specialized point-solution vendors confirms and amplifies the core structural gap identified previously—the preemptive zone is systematically underserved, and Adversary Management remains the single most critical unclaimed capability in the market.

analysis_sections.title: Adversary Lifecycle Coverage: The 86-Vendor Coverage Map
analysis_sections.body:
Mapping 86 vendor pillar scores to kill chain phases and ATT&CK tactics reveals a coverage gradient that declines sharply in the earliest adversary phases.

Exposure Management—covering kill chain Phase 1 and ATT&CK Reconnaissance—achieves the highest market penetration among the four defensive pillars, with roughly half the cohort meeting competency. This reflects broad investment in attack surface management, vulnerability prioritization, and third-party risk visibility across the cohort, including both established platform vendors and newer SaaS-native offerings.

Adversary Management—covering kill chain Phases 1 and 2 and ATT&CK Resource Development, Defense Evasion, and Credential Access—records the lowest penetration of the four defensive pillars. Only about one vendor in six reach competency, the gap to the next-weakest pillar is large, and no vendor in the cohort breaks into the advanced tier. This is the market’s most critical defensive gap: the adversary lifecycle phases where preemptive investment would have the highest incident-prevention return are the phases where market supply is thinnest.

Posture and Policy Management—covering kill chain Phases 2 and 3 and ATT&CK Initial Access and Privilege Escalation—reaches roughly a third of the cohort at threshold,. Breach and attack simulation, control validation, and cloud security posture management are present in meaningful percentages of the cohort but have not yet achieved broad penetration.

Adversary Disruption—covering kill chain Phases 4 through 7 and ATT&CK Execution through Impact—reaches approximately a third of the cohort at threshold,. Deception, threat hunting, counter-adversary operations, and managed incident response capabilities are present but variable in depth across the cohort.

Services and Capability Maturity—the cross-cutting enablement layer—reaches around 40% of the cohort at competency and about one vendor in six at the advanced platform-services tier,. The 41% services penetration rate, higher than Adversary Management, Adversary Disruption, and Posture Management, suggests that operational delivery capability is available in the market but not uniformly matched to technology strength.

Full-spectrum vendors—those meeting competency across all four defensive pillars—number under 6% of the cohort. An additional 9 vendors are near-full-spectrum with Adversary Management as the only pillar below threshold. These around 16% of the cohort represent the leading edge of the preemptive cybersecurity market.
analysis_sections.header: A coverage gradient that collapses in the preemptive zone

analysis_sections.title: The Adversary Management Bottleneck: Anatomy of an Unclaimed Market Position
analysis_sections.body:
Adversary Management is the preemptive cybersecurity pillar most directly responsible for shift-left defense—disrupting adversaries before they can deliver a weapon. Its four core sub-capabilities each address specific adversary preparation mechanisms across both frameworks.

Polymorphic and morphing defense dynamically changes the appearance and structure of the defended environment, invalidating adversary reconnaissance data. In kill chain terms this disrupts Phase 1 (Reconnaissance). In ATT&CK terms it counters Active Scanning (T1595) and Gather Victim Network Information (T1590) within the Reconnaissance tactic (TA0043).

Runtime application self-protection blocks exploitation attempts at the application layer without signature dependence, operating at Phase 2 (Weaponization) and Phase 4 (Exploitation) in kill chain terms and countering Defense Evasion (TA0005) techniques including Process Injection (T1055) and Obfuscated Files (T1027).

Dynamic network and infrastructure defense uses moving target principles to continuously alter network topology, addresses, and service configurations, frustrating adversary delivery and Command and Control establishment. This spans kill chain Phases 1, 3, and 6, and ATT&CK Command and Control (TA0011) and Delivery-phase Initial Access techniques.

Identity and credential rotation automates the rotation of credentials, API tokens, and session identifiers, rendering stolen access worthless within hours of theft. This disrupts kill chain Phases 2, 4, and 6 and counters ATT&CK Credential Access (TA0006) techniques including Brute Force (T1110) and OS Credential Dumping (T1003).

The 86-vendor data confirms that these capabilities represent the hardest and most sparsely deployed in the preemptive stack. No vendor achieves the advanced tier on Adversary Management—the threshold that signals meaningful operational deployment of two or more of these capabilities at enterprise scale. This is the clearest product-market gap identified in the full-cohort assessment, and it maps directly to the adversary lifecycle phases (Phases 1 and 2, ATT&CK Resource Development and Weaponization) where intervention yields the highest prevention return. For CPOs, this represents an unambiguous and currently unoccupied competitive position.
analysis_sections.header: Adversary Management is the unclaimed competitive position

analysis_sections.title: Services Maturity as the Operational Multiplier Across All Adversary Phases
analysis_sections.body:
The most consequential finding from the 86-vendor assessment is not which adversary phases are best or worst covered—it is the degree to which Services and Capability Maturity determines whether technology coverage is operationally real or theoretically registered.

Services maturity encompasses four dimensions. Implementation and onboarding determines how quickly and completely a vendor’s technology capability is deployed to achieve first defensive value. Consultative and advisory services determine whether findings and detections are translated into actionable customer decisions. Managed operations and continuous delivery determine whether defensive tools run with expert oversight or depend on the customer’s own operational capacity. Autonomous service delivery determines how effectively AI-driven automation scales expert-level operations to match adversary tempo.

Vendors with mature service delivery achieve a compounding advantage across the adversary lifecycle. Their Exposure Management findings become remediation programs rather than reports. Their Adversary Disruption detections trigger managed response rather than alert queues. Their Posture and Policy Management simulations generate validated control configurations rather than gap documentation. Services maturity does not change what a vendor can do—it changes what a vendor actually delivers.

The 86-vendor cohort exhibits a wider services maturity distribution than earlier assessments of the core 51 vendors, reflecting the expanded inclusion of SaaS-only platforms (typically lower services maturity) and managed service providers and consulting firms (typically higher). At competent coverage from around 40% of the cohort and with about one vendor in six reaching the advanced platform-services tier, services maturity is better distributed than most defensive pillars, but the gap between technology scores and services scores on individual vendors is often large. The strategic implication: CPOs at platform-oriented vendors must either invest in services maturity as a product capability or accept that their technology capability scores will consistently outperform their delivered defensive value—a gap that sophisticated buyers increasingly detect and discount in evaluations.
analysis_sections.header: Services maturity is the amplifier that turns coverage into delivered defense

analysis_sections.title: Delivery Model Archetypes and Their Kill Chain Profiles
analysis_sections.body:
The 86-vendor cohort encompasses a wider range of delivery models than any prior assessment, including models that did not appear in earlier evaluations of the core 51 vendors. Three classic delivery model archetypes—Platform-Only, Direct Service, and Platform-Plus-Partner—account for approximately 60% of the cohort. The remaining 40% includes SaaS platforms, managed service providers, systems integrators, consulting and advisory firms, and hybrid models that do not fit cleanly into the three classic categories.

Platform-Only vendors (25 in the cohort) lead the cohort on Posture and Policy Management and post mid-pack Exposure Management coverage, consistent with their investment in technology-led control validation and attack surface visibility. Adversary Management and services maturity are both sub-competent, confirming the structural limitation of platform-only delivery: strong Phases 1 and 3 coverage, weak Phase 2 and Phases 5–7 capability. Only a handful of platform-only vendors deliver competent Adversary Management coverage.

Direct Service vendors (11 in the cohort) show the strongest Adversary Disruption and services maturity among the three archetypes, reflecting their analyst-intensive service delivery heritage. Exposure Management and Posture and Policy Management are weaker, suggesting that while these vendors defend well in the reactive zone (Phases 4–7), they underinvest in early-phase preemptive capabilities. Adversary Management remains sub-competent even for direct service providers.

Platform-Plus-Partner vendors (15 in the cohort) show strong services maturity and Exposure Management, with weaker Posture and Policy Management and Adversary Disruption. Their model—combining platform technology with MSSP partner delivery—produces competitive early-phase coverage but inconsistent reactive-phase performance depending on partner quality and integration depth.

The additional 35 vendors in newer delivery model categories exhibit the full range of pillar profiles: some SaaS platforms show strong single-pillar scores with weak coverage elsewhere, while managed service and consulting-led vendors often show the reverse pattern. This heterogeneity reinforces the need for delivery-model-aware evaluation rather than aggregate score comparisons.

analysis_sections.title: Strategic Roadmap: Building Full Adversary Lifecycle Coverage in a 86-Vendor Market
analysis_sections.body:
The expansion from 51 to 86 assessed vendors changes the competitive context for CPOs without changing the underlying strategic priorities. The adversary lifecycle gaps identified in earlier assessments are confirmed and amplified by the larger cohort, and the first-mover advantages available to CPOs who close those gaps remain unclaimed.

Phase 1 (2026), Portfolio Mapping and Gap Quantification: Conduct a dual-framework mapping exercise to score your current portfolio against kill chain phases and ATT&CK tactics. Separately assess services maturity across all four dimensions. Identify all phases and tactics below competency. Benchmark each pillar against the cohort norm — Exposure Management leads, Adversary Management trails by a wide margin, Posture and Policy Management and Adversary Disruption sit in the middle, and Services and Capability Maturity outperforms every defensive pillar except Exposure Management. Any pillar above the cohort norm is a relative strength; any below is a structural drag on competitive positioning.

Phase 2 (2026 to 2027), Adversary Management Investment: Prioritize investment in the four Adversary Management sub-capabilities. Target competent performance to join the roughly one-in-six vendors that have cleared the bar, and set an advanced-tier target to claim a position no competitor currently holds. Simultaneously invest in services maturity to ensure new Adversary Management capabilities are operationally delivered—technology capability without operational depth produces ratings but not results.

Phase 3 (2027 to 2028), Adversary Lifecycle Positioning: Develop go-to-market messaging around kill chain phase coverage and ATT&CK tactic addressing. Build customer-facing metrics (Shift-Left Readiness Index, ATT&CK Coverage Score) that translate internal capability investments into buyer-visible outcomes. Position full adversary lifecycle coverage as the competitive standard.

Success Metrics by 2028: Adversary Management score into the advanced tier (currently unoccupied). Services maturity score into the advanced tier (achieved by 16% of the cohort). Full-spectrum coverage across all four defensive pillars — currently under 6% of the market. Customer-facing adversary lifecycle phase coverage metrics deployed across sales, marketing, and renewal conversations.

reports.background:
The Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain provides a seven-phase model of adversary behavior widely adopted by security operations teams, threat intelligence analysts, and enterprise security architects. Originally developed to analyze advanced persistent threats, the kill chain framework has become the common language for describing how attacks progress from initial reconnaissance through mission completion. The MITRE ATT&CK framework complements the kill chain with a globally accessible knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations. Its 14 enterprise tactics, mapped to hundreds of specific techniques, provide the granular detail needed to evaluate defensive coverage at the technique level.

The preemptive cybersecurity market has emerged as a category distinct from traditional detection-and-response solutions. Defined by four defensive pillars (Exposure Management, Adversary Management and Threat Intelligence, Posture and Policy Management, and Adversary Disruption) and a cross-cutting enablement layer (Services and Capability Maturity), preemptive cybersecurity aims to neutralize threats before they cause damage rather than detecting and remediating after the fact.

This version of the market insight updates the analysis from an earlier 51-vendor assessment to reflect an expanded 86-vendor cohort that includes the original evaluated vendors plus a broader range of vendor types: SaaS-native platforms, managed service providers, systems integrators, consulting and advisory firms, and specialized point-solution providers. The expanded cohort provides a more complete picture of the commercial market and surfaces structural dynamics that the smaller, more curated original cohort did not fully expose.
reports.impact:
For Chief Product Officers and Product Strategy Leaders:

The 86-vendor assessment confirms and sharpens the strategic imperatives identified in earlier assessments. CPOs face three immediate implications:

1. Portfolio Reassessment at Scale: The benchmark for competitive adequacy has shifted. In the earlier 51-vendor cohort, roughly 27% of vendors achieved full-spectrum coverage and the bar felt achievable. In the expanded 86-vendor cohort, under 6% achieve full-spectrum coverage — the bar is clearly higher and the challenge is structural. CPOs must evaluate their pillar coverage not against an idealised threshold but against the actual distribution of the expanded market — where Exposure Management leads, Adversary Management trails by a wide margin, and no vendor has claimed the advanced tier on Adversary Management.

2. Adversary Management as Primary Investment Priority: With 0 of 86 vendors into the advanced tier on Adversary Management, this is the clearest unoccupied competitive position in the market. The investment case is straightforward: the capabilities required are technically defined, the competitive position is unclaimed, and buyer demand for earliest-phase preemptive defense is increasing as MITRE ATT&CK evaluations mature.

3. Services Maturity as a Mandatory Investment: The expanded cohort includes many vendors with strong technology scores and weak operational delivery. In a buyer market that increasingly evaluates vendors on outcome delivery rather than feature capability, services maturity investment is no longer optional. CPOs who deprioritize services maturity in favor of technology feature velocity will find their measured capability coverage increasingly disconnected from buyer-perceived value.

For Technology and Engineering Leaders:

Engineering roadmaps should prioritize the four Adversary Management sub-capabilities (polymorphic defense, runtime application protection, dynamic infrastructure defense, credential rotation) as technically demanding but strategically critical investments. These capabilities require systems-level expertise in runtime instrumentation, network manipulation, and cryptographic automation—skills that cannot be acquired through product management decisions alone and represent durable competitive moats.

For Corporate Development and Strategy Leaders:

Acquisition strategy should target the Adversary Management gap as the primary value-creation thesis. Any acquisition that delivers credible capability above competency on Adversary Management creates cross-pillar value by enabling full-spectrum positioning. Secondary acquisition value lies in services maturity—acquisitions that add managed operations depth amplify the delivered value of every existing technology pillar simultaneously.
reports.conclusion:
Expanding the preemptive cybersecurity assessment to 86 vendors confirms the structural thesis while sharpening its edge. The kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK dual-framework analysis reveals a market that is growing in scale and vendor diversity but not yet in the depth of capability that defines genuine shift-left defense. Exposure Management has achieved meaningful market penetration. Services maturity is present in over 40% of the cohort. But Adversary Management—the pillar that addresses the earliest and most prevention-valuable adversary lifecycle phases—remains at 16% penetration with no vendor at the advanced tier.

For CPOs, the strategic imperative is unchanged from prior assessments but more urgent: the window for first-mover advantage on Adversary Management is open, the competitive space is unoccupied, and the buyer demand for genuine preemptive—not just pre-detection—capability is accelerating. Services maturity investment remains the force multiplier that converts technology capability into defensible market positioning.

The vendors who will define the next generation of preemptive cybersecurity are not those with the broadest feature catalogs or the largest vendor cohort coverage ratings. They are those that combine genuine Adversary Management capability—disrupting adversaries at Phases 1 and 2, countering Resource Development and Defense Evasion—with the operational services depth to deliver those capabilities reliably at enterprise scale. In an 86-vendor market where full-spectrum coverage remains below 6%, the competitive ceiling is still unclaimed.

analysis_sections.header: Finding 1 → Recommendation 1: Adversary Management is the unclaimed pillar
analysis_sections.title: Adversary Management: the highest-leverage gap nobody owns
analysis_sections.body:
**Every assessed vendor is sub-competent in Adversary Management, and not a single vendor sits in the advanced tier.** That makes it the largest unclaimed competitive position in the preemptive stack.

**Why it matters.** Adversary Management is where defenders disrupt attackers *before* a weapon is delivered: the shift-left dividend. An empty advanced tier means the buyer cannot point to a market leader, so the first credible entrant defines the category.

**By the numbers.**
- Roughly **one in eight** vendors clears competency on Adversary Management.
- **Zero** vendors reach the advanced tier across the four Adversary Management sub-capabilities.
- Coverage is thinnest on polymorphic defense, runtime self-protection, dynamic network manipulation, and automated credential rotation.

**What to do.** Direct your next two engineering cycles at the four Adversary Management sub-capabilities and validate quarterly coverage gains against ATT&CK Resource Development (TA0042), Defense Evasion (TA0005), and Credential Access (TA0006).

**The bottom line.** Whoever ships first in Adversary Management writes the category definition the rest of the market has to answer.

analysis_sections.header: Finding 2 → Recommendation 2: Full-spectrum coverage is rare
analysis_sections.title: The full-spectrum gap: under six percent cover all four pillars
analysis_sections.body:
**No vendor currently clears competency across all four defensive pillars.** A small leadership cluster of roughly 9% of the market is pulling ahead of the rest.

**Why it matters.** Buyers asking for end-to-end adversary lifecycle coverage are choosing from a very short list. If you are not on it, you are competing on individual pillars against vendors who can lead with the whole story.

**By the numbers.**
- **0%** of the assessed vendors clear competency on all four pillars (Exposure Management, Adversary Management, Posture and Policy Management, Adversary Disruption).
- **~9%** form the leadership cluster pulling decisively ahead.
- The remainder cover one or two pillars at most.

**What to do.** Map your portfolio to all seven kill chain phases and the 14 MITRE ATT&CK tactics within 60 days, tag every capability as competent or sub-competent against the market norm, and publish the heat map as your investment-case single source of truth.

**The bottom line.** The leadership cluster is small and reachable: but only if full-spectrum becomes an explicit 18-month commitment, not a marketing claim.

analysis_sections.header: Finding 3 → Recommendation 3: The dual-framework lens validates the taxonomy
analysis_sections.title: Kill chain phases meet ATT&CK tactics: and the preemptive zone is weakest
analysis_sections.body:
**Mapping the market coverage data to both the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK produces the same picture: preemptive coverage collapses where vendors should be strongest.** Two independent frameworks agreeing means the gap is structural, not measurement noise.

**Why it matters.** When you reframe the buying conversation around adversary lifecycle phases instead of feature catalogs, you control the framework the buyer scores you on: and that framework rewards your investments in the preemptive zone.

**By the numbers.**
- Highest market penetration sits at **Phase 1 (Reconnaissance / Exposure Management)**, where roughly half the market meets competency.
- **Phases 2–3 (Weaponization, Delivery)** are the weakest in the preemptive zone.
- ATT&CK tactic coverage mirrors the kill chain phase coverage almost perfectly.

**What to do.** Rewrite sales engineering decks, pricing pages, and demo scripts around phase coverage and tactic disruption rates, and train every customer-facing role to lead with that framing in the first ten minutes of any opportunity.

**The bottom line.** Two frameworks, one verdict: own the framing and the score follows.

analysis_sections.header: Finding 4 → Recommendation 4: Services maturity is the amplifier
analysis_sections.title: Services and Capability Maturity turn coverage into delivered defense
analysis_sections.body:
**Most vendors meet the basic Services and Capability Maturity threshold, but strong services delivery remains the true differentiator: only about a third of the market achieves it.** Without services maturity, a strong pillar score is theoretical.

**Why it matters.** Services is the connective tissue across Exposure Management, Adversary Management, Posture and Policy Management, and Adversary Disruption. Buyers feel the gap in onboarding velocity, in advisory depth, in 24/7 operations, and in how much of the response is automated.

**By the numbers.**
- **~86%** of the market meets the basic Services and Capability Maturity threshold; only **~34%** reach strong services delivery.
- The largest service-side gaps cluster in **autonomous AI-driven delivery** and **consultative advisory**.
- Vendors strong in services convert pillar coverage into measurable outcomes far more reliably than peers.

**What to do.** Fund the four services dimensions in parallel: implementation, advisory, 24/7 managed operations, and AI-driven delivery: and tie services-maturity goals to pillar-coverage outcomes so the gap between potential and production closes by the next reporting cycle.

**The bottom line.** Services is not a side bet. It is the multiplier on every other investment in the portfolio.

analysis_sections.header: Finding 5 → Recommendation 5: Three delivery archetypes, three coverage profiles
analysis_sections.title: Same pillar score, different meaning: archetype context matters
analysis_sections.body:
**The market divides into three structurally different delivery archetypes, and the same headline pillar score means different things in each.** Comparing vendors without archetype context produces misleading conclusions.

**Why it matters.** Buyers and CPOs who skip the archetype step end up comparing a managed-service operator with a pure platform vendor on the same axis: the resulting battle card is wrong before it leaves the building.

**By the numbers.**
- **Platform-Only, Direct Service, and Platform-Plus-Partner** archetypes account for roughly **60%** of the market.
- The remaining **~40%** spans SaaS platforms, MSSPs, systems integrators, and integrated platform-plus-service models.
- Coverage profiles differ most sharply in **Services and Adversary Disruption**, the pillars where delivery model dominates outcomes.

**What to do.** Classify your organisation and every key competitor by archetype before any pillar comparison, structure battle cards and pricing inside archetype peer groups, and lead customer conversations with archetype context so buyers see why coverage differs by vendor *type*, not just vendor.

**The bottom line.** Archetype-aware comparisons are the difference between a defensible positioning story and an apples-to-oranges debate.

analysis_sections.header: Finding 6 → Recommendation 6: ATT&CK tactic-level gaps mirror the kill chain
analysis_sections.title: TA0042, TA0005, and TA0006 are the under-served tactics that decide preemptive credibility
analysis_sections.body:
**ATT&CK tactic-level coverage mirrors the kill chain almost one-for-one, and three tactics consistently emerge as the most under-served across the market.** Late-phase tactic effectiveness then tracks services maturity, not technology depth.

**Why it matters.** Buyers increasingly run RFPs and renewal conversations in ATT&CK terms. Vendors who can quantify tactic-level disruption rates: and pair those rates with the services dimension behind them: win the credibility argument.

**By the numbers.**
- The three most under-served tactics across assessed vendors are **TA0042 (Resource Development)**, **TA0005 (Defense Evasion)**, and **TA0006 (Credential Access)**.
- Late-phase tactics (**TA0008–TA0011**) show effectiveness that varies *with services maturity*, not just product capability.
- Tactic coverage and kill chain phase coverage agree across the market, confirming the structural gap.

**What to do.** Build a quarterly tactic-coverage report that quantifies disruption rates for TA0042 / TA0005 / TA0006 and for the late-phase tactics, pair each rate with its supporting services dimension, and surface the report in renewal conversations, RFP responses, and customer business reviews.

**The bottom line.** Tactic-level metrics with services context is the language the next generation of buyers will use: publish it first.

reports.background:
The Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain provides a seven-phase model of adversary behavior widely adopted by security operations teams, threat intelligence analysts, and enterprise security architects. Originally developed to analyze advanced persistent threats, the kill chain framework has become the common language for describing how attacks progress from initial reconnaissance through mission completion. The MITRE ATT&CK framework complements the kill chain with a globally accessible knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations. Its 14 enterprise tactics, mapped to hundreds of specific techniques, provide the granular detail needed to evaluate defensive coverage at the technique level.

The preemptive cybersecurity market has emerged as a category distinct from traditional detection-and-response solutions. Defined by four defensive pillars (Exposure Management, Adversary Management and Threat Intelligence, Posture and Policy Management, and Adversary Disruption) and a cross-cutting enablement layer (Services and Capability Maturity), preemptive cybersecurity aims to neutralize threats before they cause damage rather than detecting and remediating after the fact.

The assessed vendor set spans a broad range of vendor types: SaaS-native platforms, managed service providers, systems integrators, consulting and advisory firms, and specialized point-solution providers. This breadth provides a representative picture of the commercial market and surfaces structural dynamics across delivery archetypes, technology approaches, and services maturity levels.
reports.impact:
**Why this matters for product and engineering leaders.** The data makes the gaps unambiguous and the opportunities sequenceable.

- **Adversary Management** is the highest-leverage move: no advanced-tier incumbent exists.
- **Full-spectrum coverage** is the price of entry to the leadership cluster.
- **Services maturity** is the multiplier that turns either of the above into delivered defense.
- **Archetype context** is the lens that keeps competitive comparisons honest.
- **Tactic-level reporting** is the credibility currency for the next buying cycle.
reports.conclusion:
**The data is unambiguous and the opportunity is sequenceable.** The preemptive zone is wide open, the leadership cluster is small, and services maturity is what separates a coverage claim from a delivered outcome.

**For CPOs.** Pick the finding-to-recommendation pair that hurts most, fund it, and instrument it. The first vendor to combine full-pillar coverage with credible services maturity and published ATT&CK tactic-level disruption rates will define the category.

glossary.definition: The upper band of capability where a vendor demonstrates meaningful operational deployment of two or more sub-capabilities at enterprise scale. No vendor in the market currently sits in the advanced tier for Adversary Management.

Deception, threat hunting, counter-adversary operations, containment, and incident response. Maps to kill chain Phases 4 through 7 and ATT&CK Execution (TA0002), Persistence (TA0003), Lateral Movement (TA0008), Command and Control (TA0011), Collection (TA0009), Exfiltration (TA0010), and Impact (TA0040). Delivered competently by roughly a fifth of assessed vendors.

Polymorphic defense, moving-target defense, runtime application self-protection, and credential rotation. Maps to kill chain Phases 1 and 2 and ATT&CK Resource Development (TA0042), Defense Evasion (TA0005), and Credential Access (TA0006). The structural bottleneck of the market: competency reached by only about one vendor in eight, with no vendor in the advanced tier.

A prolonged, targeted intrusion in which an adversary establishes covert presence in a network to achieve strategic objectives. The kill chain framework was originally developed to analyse APT campaigns.

The 14 enterprise tactics in MITRE ATT&CK: Reconnaissance, Resource Development, Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defense Evasion, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Collection, Exfiltration, Command and Control, and Impact.

Automated, continuous emulation of adversary techniques against production controls to validate that defensive configurations behave as intended. A core capability of the Posture and Policy Management pillar.
The executive accountable for product strategy, roadmap, and lifecycle outcomes. The primary audience for this research.

A capability dimension that amplifies or diminishes the effectiveness of every phase-mapped defensive pillar without mapping to specific adversary lifecycle phases itself. Services and Capability Maturity is the primary cross-cutting enablement layer in the preemptive cybersecurity taxonomy.
Continuous monitoring and remediation of misconfigurations and policy drift in public-cloud environments. A core capability of the Posture and Policy Management pillar.

Lockheed Martin's seven-phase model of adversary behaviour: Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, and Actions on Objectives. Used to map defensive capabilities to specific adversary actions.

The commercial form a vendor uses to deliver capability: for example platform-only, direct service, platform-plus-partner, SaaS, MSSP, consulting-led, or integrated platform-plus-service. The same pillar coverage rating can represent fundamentally different operational realities across delivery models.

Continuous discovery, prioritisation, and remediation of exploitable vulnerabilities and attack surface exposures. Maps to kill chain Phase 1 and ATT&CK Reconnaissance (TA0043) and Discovery (TA0007). The best-covered defensive pillar in the market, with roughly half of vendors delivering competent coverage.

The preemptive cybersecurity capability framework used in this research: four defensive pillars. Exposure Management, Adversary Management, Posture and Policy Management, and Adversary Disruption: plus a cross-cutting enablement layer, Services and Capability Maturity.
A vendor delivering competent coverage on all four defensive pillars (Exposure Management, Adversary Management, Adversary Disruption, PPM). No assessed vendor currently qualifies.
The combined set of full-spectrum vendors and near-full-spectrum vendors. Roughly 9% of the market.

A globally accessible knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures based on real-world observations. Provides 14 enterprise tactics and hundreds of specific techniques that complement the kill chain's linear model with granular technique-level detail.

A defensive strategy that continuously changes the attack surface: addresses, configurations, identities, or code: to increase adversary cost and complexity. A core Adversary Management capability mapping to kill chain Phase 1 and ATT&CK Reconnaissance (TA0043).

A vendor that operates security capabilities on behalf of customers, typically including monitoring, detection, and response. MSSPs in these providers generally pair higher services maturity with variable technology depth.

A vendor delivering competent coverage on Exposure Management, Adversary Disruption, and Posture and Policy Management but sub-competent coverage on Adversary Management: the most common gap pattern in the market.

Breach and attack simulation, security control validation, penetration testing, and cloud security posture management. Maps to kill chain Phases 2 and 3 and ATT&CK Initial Access (TA0001) and Privilege Escalation (TA0004). Delivered competently by roughly a third of assessed vendors.

Kill chain Phases 1 through 3 (Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery) and the corresponding early-lifecycle ATT&CK tactics, where preemptive capabilities prevent attacks before exploitation occurs. The weakest-defended region of the adversary lifecycle across the market.
In-process application instrumentation that detects and blocks exploitation attempts at runtime without depending on external signature databases. A core Adversary Management sub-capability.

The MITRE ATT&CK tactic describing adversary infrastructure building, exploit development, and capability acquisition. The ATT&CK tactic with the weakest vendor coverage in the market, dependent on Adversary Management capabilities.

A vendor-hosted, multi-tenant delivery model in which customers access capability through a cloud-delivered application. Common among platform-only vendors in the assessed market, typically paired with lower services maturity.

Implementation and onboarding, consultative advisory, managed operations, and autonomous AI-driven delivery. The cross-cutting enablement layer that determines whether each defensive pillar is operationally delivered. Most assessed vendors meet the basic services threshold; strong services delivery is achieved by roughly a third of the market, with about one in ten in the advanced platform-services tier.
The strategic movement of defensive investment from later adversary lifecycle phases (detection and response after exploitation) to earlier phases (prevention and disruption before exploitation).

evidence: Gartner Preemptive Cybersecurity Vendor Assessment, 2025–2026: vendor evaluation across 4 defensive pillars, 1 cross-cutting services maturity dimension, and 24 sub-pillar dimensions. Vendor grade distribution: A 87%, B 3%, C 5%, D 5%.

Overall pillar competency rates (assessed vendors): Exposure Management covered competently by roughly half of assessed vendors; Adversary Management by about one vendor in eight with no vendor in the advanced tier; Posture and Policy Management by approximately a third; Adversary Disruption by approximately a fifth; Services and Capability Maturity: approximately 86% of assessed vendors meet the basic threshold, roughly a third achieve strong services delivery, and about one in ten operate at the advanced platform-services tier. Full-spectrum coverage across all four defensive pillars: no vendor currently qualifies. Near-full-spectrum (Adversary Management as the lone gap): an additional ~9% of the market.

Delivery-model breakdown (the assessed vendors across three classic archetypes): Platform-Only, roughly half the market leading on Posture and Policy Management and competitive on Exposure Management, sub-competent on Adversary Management. Direct Service, roughly a quarter strongest on Adversary Disruption and Services maturity, weaker on early-phase pillars. Platform-Plus-Partner, roughly a quarter strongest on Services maturity and Exposure Management, weaker on Posture and Policy Management and Adversary Disruption.
Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain (Hutchins, Cloppert, Amin, 2011): Intelligence-Driven Computer Network Defense Informed by Analysis of Adversary Campaigns and Intrusion Kill Chains.

MITRE ATT&CK Framework v14 (2024): Enterprise tactics and techniques knowledge base. 14 enterprise tactics mapped to four defensive pillars; Services and Capability Maturity treated as a cross-cutting enablement layer separate from tactic mapping.
NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 (2024): Cross-referenced to ensure alignment with Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover functions.
